title: The Promise That Bought a Vote

pages.text: In the fictional market town of Asasekro, excitement filled the air as residents prepared to elect a community representative to the local council. Fourteen-year-old Kofi and his classmate Ama walked home from JHS with their civic-club notebooks. Yet right outside their school, they stepped carefully over a broken footbridge and passed a community clinic whose roof leaked every rainy season.
sentences: In the fictional market town of Asasekro, excitement filled the air as residents prepared to elect a community representative to the local council.
Fourteen-year-old Kofi and his classmate Ama walked home from JHS with their civic-club notebooks.
Yet right outside their school, they stepped carefully over a broken footbridge and passed a community clinic whose roof leaked every rainy season.
pages.alt: Fourteen-year-old Kofi and Ama walk with their notebooks past a cracked wooden footbridge and a small clinic in the fictional town of Asasekro.

pages.text: That afternoon at the town lorry park, a loud music van arrived for Candidate A’s rally. Assistants handed out free packets of food and fifty-cedi notes to cheering bystanders while Candidate A shouted into a microphone: ‘Vote for me on Saturday, and within three months I will build a giant glass shopping mall, a stadium, and pave every lane in Asasekro!’ Kofi’s older cousin, Uncle Yaw, pocketed a gift packet with a grin.

pages.alt: At a crowded lorry park rally, assistants hand out small gift packets while a speaker on a platform gestures grandly.

pages.text: An hour later under the community centre shade trees, Candidate B held a quieter town-hall meeting. Instead of handing out cash or gifts, she distributed a printed two-page sheet showing the local council’s real annual capital budget and answered tough questions from farmers, teachers and traders. Several people in the back yawned and walked away because there were no free handouts.

pages.alt: Under shade trees at the community centre, a female candidate explains a budget chart to attentive townspeople while a few people walk away.

pages.text: On the walk home, Uncle Yaw held up his gift packet. ‘Candidate A already gave me something today!’ he said. ‘Why shouldn’t I vote for the person who shares gifts right now?’ Ama stopped and opened her notebook. ‘Uncle Yaw, let us test that idea using maths and civic facts before you decide.’

‘Candidate A already gave me something today!’ he said.

‘Uncle Yaw, let us test that idea using maths and civic facts before you decide.’
pages.alt: Uncle Yaw holds up his gift packet while Ama and Kofi open their notebooks on the family veranda.

pages.text: The next morning in Social Studies class, Mrs Mensah explained how public projects are actually funded. ‘No elected leader pays for roads, clinics or bridges out of their personal pocket,’ she said. ‘Public infrastructure is paid for by citizens’ taxes and statutory funds allocated through an approved public budget. To judge whether a campaign promise is credible, citizens must check the numbers!’

‘Public infrastructure is paid for by citizens’ taxes and statutory funds allocated through an approved public budget.
To judge whether a campaign promise is credible, citizens must check the numbers!’
pages.alt: In the JHS classroom, Mrs Mensah points to a diagram showing taxes flowing into a public budget for clinics, water and roads.

pages.text: With Mrs Mensah’s guidance, the civic club inspected the published District Assembly budget summary at the library. Asasekro’s entire annual capital budget for local works was five hundred thousand cedis. Candidate A’s promised stadium and glass mall would cost over five million cedis — ten times the entire budget, with zero explanation of where the money would come from!

pages.alt: Kofi and Ama compare the official council budget binder with the cost of the promised projects using a calculator.

pages.text: Next, they checked Candidate B’s written plan. Fixing the leaking clinic roof cost one hundred and twenty thousand cedis, repairing the school footbridge cost eighty thousand cedis, and drilling two solar boreholes cost one hundred thousand cedis — three hundred thousand cedis in total, leaving two hundred thousand cedis for maintenance and drainage. Every cedi was accounted for within the real budget!

Every cedi was accounted for within the real budget!
pages.alt: Ama traces the three costed items—clinic roof, footbridge and boreholes—totalling 300,000 cedis within the 500,000-cedi budget.

pages.text: That evening, Kofi showed Uncle Yaw another calculation. ‘A council term lasts four years — about one thousand four hundred and sixty days,’ Kofi said. ‘If someone gives a voter fifty cedis to buy their vote for four years, that works out to less than four pesewas a day! Worse still, a politician who buys votes with private cash often treats office as a business to recover their money instead of serving the town.’

Worse still, a politician who buys votes with private cash often treats office as a business to recover their money instead of serving the town.’
pages.alt: Kofi shows Uncle Yaw on a calculator how 50 cedis divided across four years (1,460 days) is less than four pesewas a day.

pages.text: On Thursday evening, the Asasekro Youth and Elders Association hosted a non-partisan community debate. Citizens respectfully asked both candidates three factual questions: What is the exact cost of your top priority? Which budget line will fund it? And how will you report progress every six months? When pressed for evidence, uncosted slogans quickly stood apart from realistic plans.

When pressed for evidence, uncosted slogans quickly stood apart from realistic plans.
pages.alt: At a peaceful community forum, townspeople ask calm, evidence-based questions of the candidates seated on stage.

pages.text: At the forum, Uncle Yaw’s friend whispered, ‘What if people get angry because we support different candidates?’ Mrs Mensah reminded the audience of a vital constitutional principle: ‘In a democracy, citizens can disagree on policies while remaining neighbours and friends. Even more importantly, the ballot is secret — nobody inside the voting booth can see whom you choose, so no gift or threat can force your hand.’

Even more importantly, the ballot is secret — nobody inside the voting booth can see whom you choose, so no gift or threat can force your hand.’
pages.alt: Mrs Mensah points to a demonstration cardboard voting screen showing how every voter marks their ballot in complete privacy.

pages.text: After the election, Kofi and Ama learned that citizenship does not end on voting day! Whether a candidate wins or loses, residents must attend town-hall budget hearings, inspect public project noticeboards, and track accountability — requiring leaders to explain how public funds are spent and whether promised milestones are met.
sentences: After the election, Kofi and Ama learned that citizenship does not end on voting day!

Whether a candidate wins or loses, residents must attend town-hall budget hearings, inspect public project noticeboards, and track accountability — requiring leaders to explain how public funds are spent and whether promised milestones are met.
pages.alt: Kofi, Ama, Uncle Yaw and townspeople inspect a public project progress board outside the newly repaired clinic roof.

pages.text: Walking across the newly repaired school footbridge a few months later, Kofi and Ama smiled. No single politician could magically fix every problem overnight, and good leaders deserved respect when they worked honestly — just as citizens deserved truth, clear budgets and real accountability. A strong Ghana, they realised, begins with minds that cannot be bought.

activities.question: Why did Kofi and Ama conclude that Candidate A’s 5-million-cedi promise was not credible?
options: Asasekro’s entire annual capital budget was only 500,000 cedis
The town had no space to plant a single tree
Public projects are always paid from a teacher’s pocket
activities.explanation: A 5,000,000-cedi promise was ten times the town’s entire 500,000-cedi capital budget, with no funding source explained.

activities.definition: Believable and trustworthy because it is supported by evidence and realistic numbers
distractors: Loudly announced through a music van loudspeaker
Kept secret from taxpayers and voters

activities.question: How much did Candidate B’s three priority projects (120,000 + 80,000 + 100,000 cedis) cost in total?
options: 300,000 cedis, fitting within the 500,000-cedi capital budget
5,000,000 cedis, ten times more than the budget

activities.question: How does the secret ballot protect voters during an election?
options: No one sees your vote in the booth, so gifts cannot force your choice
Only two people in the town are allowed to know the election date
Voters must whisper their choice to a loudspeaker
activities.explanation: Because the ballot is secret, each citizen votes privately according to their conscience and judgment.

activities.prompt: Order the steps of responsible civic decision-making shown in the story.
items: Identify real community needs like the clinic roof and footbridge.
Compare campaign promises against the official published budget.
Vote independently and follow up on public project accountability.
